CHAPTER 19 - REPRODUCTION IN PLANTS

Introduction

Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. It ensures the continuity of a species from one generation to the next and, through the reshuffling of characters, provides the variation on which evolution acts. Plants, being the primary producers of the living world, show a remarkable diversity of reproductive strategies. Some plants multiply without any fusion of reproductive cells, while others produce seeds only after male and female gametes unite. This chapter examines the modes of reproduction in plants: asexual reproduction and vegetative propagation, and sexual reproduction in flowering plants (angiosperms) - the structure of the flower, the formation of pollen grains (microsporogenesis) and of the embryo sac (megasporogenesis), pollination, the unique event of double fertilization, and the development of the seed and fruit.

19.1 MODES OF REPRODUCTION

Broadly, reproduction in plants is of two kinds. In ASEXUAL reproduction a single parent gives rise to offspring WITHOUT the formation and fusion of gametes; the new individuals are genetically IDENTICAL to the parent and to one another, forming a CLONE. In SEXUAL reproduction two gametes - a male and a female - fuse to form a zygote, which develops into a new individual; the offspring inherit characters from both parents and therefore show VARIATION. Asexual reproduction is rapid and needs only one parent, making it useful where conditions are stable; sexual reproduction is slower but generates the variability that helps a species adapt and survive changing environments.

19.2 ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION

Asexual reproduction takes several forms, especially in simple plants, algae and fungi.

(a) FISSION. In unicellular organisms the parent cell divides into two (binary fission) or many (multiple fission) daughter cells. Unicellular algae such as diatoms and organisms like bacteria reproduce this way. In binary fission the nucleus divides first, followed by the cytoplasm, giving two equal daughters.

(b) BUDDING. A small outgrowth, or bud, appears on the parent body, grows, and eventually separates to form a new individual. YEAST, a unicellular fungus, is the classic example: a bud pinches off from the parent cell and may itself bud before detaching, forming short chains.

(c) FRAGMENTATION. The body of the organism breaks into two or more fragments, and each fragment grows into a complete new organism. The filamentous green alga SPIROGYRA reproduces by fragmentation - its filaments break and each piece develops into a new filament. Many mosses and liverworts also spread this way.

(d) SPORE FORMATION. Many plants and fungi produce tiny, light, thick-walled reproductive units called SPORES inside a sporangium. Spores are dispersed by wind or water; on reaching a suitable place each germinates into a new plant WITHOUT fusing with any other cell. The bread mould RHIZOPUS forms spores in a sporangium borne on an upright hypha; ferns and mosses also reproduce by spores. Spores allow rapid multiplication and help the organism survive unfavourable conditions.

19.3 VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION

Vegetative propagation is a form of asexual reproduction in higher plants in which a VEGETATIVE part of the plant - a root, stem, leaf or bud - detaches and grows into a new, independent plant. Because no gametes are involved, the new plants are genetically identical to the parent. Vegetative propagation may be NATURAL or ARTIFICIAL.

NATURAL METHODS use structures the plant produces on its own:
 - RUNNERS (stolons): slender horizontal stems that creep along the ground; at their nodes they strike roots and raise new shoots, as in grass, strawberry and Oxalis.
 - RHIZOMES: thick, horizontal underground stems bearing buds; each bud can grow into a new shoot, as in ginger, turmeric and banana.
 - BULBS: short underground stems surrounded by fleshy leaf bases storing food, with buds that form new plants, as in onion, garlic and lily.
 - TUBERS: swollen underground stem tips storing food and bearing 'eyes' (buds), as in the potato; each eye can sprout a new plant.
 - OFFSETS: short lateral branches that arise from the base of the parent and form new plantlets, as in water hyacinth (Eichhornia) and Pistia.
Some plants propagate by LEAVES: the leaf margins of Bryophyllum bear buds (adventitious buds) that fall and grow into new plants.

ARTIFICIAL METHODS are practised by gardeners and horticulturists to multiply useful plants quickly and to keep desirable characters unchanged:
 - CUTTING: a piece of stem, root or leaf with buds is cut and planted; it develops roots and grows into a new plant, as in rose, sugarcane, Bougainvillea and money plant.
 - LAYERING: a lower branch is bent to the ground and part of it is covered with moist soil; after it forms roots, the rooted portion is cut from the parent and grown separately, as in jasmine, lemon and guava.
 - GRAFTING: parts of two plants are joined so that they unite and grow as one. The rooted lower plant is the STOCK and the cut shoot inserted into it is the SCION; grafting combines the strong root system of one plant with the desirable fruit or flower of another, as in mango, apple and rose.
 - TISSUE CULTURE (MICROPROPAGATION): small pieces of plant tissue (explants) are grown on a sterile nutrient medium containing plant hormones. Because plant cells are TOTIPOTENT (a single cell can regenerate a whole plant), thousands of identical plantlets can be raised from a tiny amount of tissue in a small space and a short time. This technique is used to multiply orchids, banana and many ornamental and disease-free crop plants.

Vegetative propagation has clear ADVANTAGES: it is quicker than growing from seed, it produces plants identical to the parent so good qualities are retained, and it allows plants that produce few or no viable seeds (such as banana, sugarcane and seedless grapes) to be multiplied. Its main LIMITATION is that it produces no variation, so a whole crop of clones can be wiped out by a single disease.

19.4 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS

In flowering plants (angiosperms) the FLOWER is the organ of sexual reproduction. Sexual reproduction involves the formation of male gametes (in pollen grains) and female gametes (in the embryo sac), their coming together by pollination, their fusion by fertilization, and the development of seeds and fruits.

STRUCTURE OF A FLOWER. A typical flower is borne on a stalk, the PEDICEL, which widens at the top into the THALAMUS (receptacle) on which the floral parts are arranged in whorls. From outside inwards there are four whorls:
 1. CALYX - the outermost whorl of green, leaf-like SEPALS. The calyx protects the young flower in the bud and, being green, may also photosynthesise.
 2. COROLLA - the whorl of PETALS, usually brightly coloured and often scented and rich in nectar. The corolla attracts insects and birds for pollination.
 3. ANDROECIUM - the male whorl, made of STAMENS. Each stamen has a stalk, the FILAMENT, bearing a two-lobed ANTHER at its tip. The anther contains pollen sacs in which pollen grains are produced.
 4. GYNOECIUM (pistil) - the female whorl, made of one or more CARPELS. Each carpel has three parts: a swollen basal OVARY containing ovules, a slender STYLE rising from the ovary, and a sticky tip, the STIGMA, which receives the pollen.
A flower having all four whorls is COMPLETE; one bearing both androecium and gynoecium is BISEXUAL (perfect). The calyx and corolla are the ACCESSORY whorls (they aid reproduction); the androecium and gynoecium are the ESSENTIAL whorls (they actually produce gametes).

19.5 MICROSPOROGENESIS AND POLLEN

MICROSPOROGENESIS is the process of formation of microspores (pollen grains) inside the anther. A young anther is four-lobed and contains four POLLEN SACS (microsporangia). Each pollen sac is packed with many diploid MICROSPORE MOTHER CELLS (pollen mother cells). Each pollen mother cell undergoes MEIOSIS, dividing to form a group of four haploid cells called a TETRAD of microspores. The microspores separate, enlarge and develop into POLLEN GRAINS.

STRUCTURE OF A POLLEN GRAIN. A mature pollen grain has a two-layered wall: a tough, sculptured outer layer, the EXINE, made of a very resistant substance (sporopollenin), and a thin inner layer, the INTINE, of cellulose and pectin. The exine has thin areas called germ pores through which the pollen tube later emerges. Inside, the pollen grain (the male gametophyte) contains two cells - a large VEGETATIVE (tube) CELL and a small GENERATIVE CELL. The generative cell later divides to form two MALE GAMETES. Pollen grains are light and produced in enormous numbers, which aids their dispersal.

19.6 MEGASPOROGENESIS AND THE EMBRYO SAC

MEGASPOROGENESIS is the process of formation of the megaspore, which gives rise to the female gametophyte (the embryo sac), and takes place inside the OVULE. An ovule is a small body attached to the ovary wall by a stalk called the FUNICLE. The main body of the ovule is the NUCELLUS, surrounded by one or two protective coats, the INTEGUMENTS, which leave a small opening at one end called the MICROPYLE. The point where the integuments, nucellus and funicle meet is the CHALAZA.

Within the nucellus a single diploid MEGASPORE MOTHER CELL undergoes MEIOSIS to produce four haploid megaspores arranged in a row. Usually THREE of them degenerate and only ONE functional megaspore survives. The functional megaspore enlarges and its nucleus divides mitotically three times to give EIGHT nuclei. These eight nuclei organise into the mature EMBRYO SAC (female gametophyte), a seven-celled, eight-nucleate structure: at the micropylar end an EGG APPARATUS of three cells - one EGG CELL (the female gamete) flanked by two SYNERGIDS; at the opposite (chalazal) end three ANTIPODAL cells; and in the centre a large CENTRAL CELL containing two POLAR NUCLEI that fuse to form a diploid SECONDARY NUCLEUS. Thus the embryo sac carries the egg that will be fertilized and the polar nuclei that will give rise to the endosperm.

19.7 POLLINATION

POLLINATION is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. It is a necessary step before fertilization because the male gametes are enclosed in the pollen and must be brought to the female part. Pollination is of two types.

SELF-POLLINATION (autogamy) is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the SAME flower or another flower of the same plant. It is possible only in bisexual flowers, ensures seed set even when pollinating agents are few, keeps the parental characters pure, but produces little variation. Many peas and wheat flowers are self-pollinated.

CROSS-POLLINATION (allogamy) is the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of a flower on a DIFFERENT plant of the same species. It introduces variation and produces more vigorous offspring, but depends on an external agent and may waste much pollen. Plants favour cross-pollination through devices such as unisexual flowers, the anther and stigma maturing at different times, and self-incompatibility.

AGENTS OF POLLINATION. Because pollen cannot move on its own, cross-pollination needs a carrier:
 - WIND (ANEMOPHILY): wind-pollinated flowers are usually small, dull and without scent or nectar; they produce enormous quantities of light, dry pollen and have large, often feathery stigmas and versatile anthers that expose the pollen to the wind, as in grasses, maize and many trees.
 - WATER (HYDROPHILY): a few aquatic plants, such as Vallisneria and Hydrilla, use water to carry pollen to the stigma; their pollen is often long and unwettable.
 - INSECTS (ENTOMOPHILY): insect-pollinated flowers are large or clustered, brightly coloured, scented and provide nectar as a reward; their pollen is sticky or spiny and the stigma is sticky, so pollen clings to the insect's body and is carried from flower to flower. Bees, butterflies, moths and beetles are common insect pollinators. Some flowers are also pollinated by birds (ornithophily) and bats.
These features are ADAPTATIONS that match a flower to its pollinator and improve the chance of successful pollination.

19.8 DOUBLE FERTILIZATION

After pollination, the pollen grain on the stigma absorbs moisture and germinates, putting out a POLLEN TUBE that grows down through the style, guided towards the ovule, and enters the embryo sac usually through the micropyle. The tube carries the two male gametes. There it discharges them, and TWO fusions take place - a process unique to angiosperms called DOUBLE FERTILIZATION:
 - SYNGAMY (true fertilization): one male gamete fuses with the EGG CELL to form a diploid ZYGOTE (2n), which develops into the EMBRYO of the new plant.
 - TRIPLE FUSION: the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei (the secondary nucleus) of the central cell to form a TRIPLOID (3n) PRIMARY ENDOSPERM NUCLEUS, which develops into the ENDOSPERM, a nutritive tissue that feeds the growing embryo.
Because one fertilization gives the zygote and the other gives the endosperm, the term DOUBLE fertilization is used, and because three nuclei fuse in the second event it is called triple fusion. Double fertilization ensures that endosperm (food) is formed only when an embryo is also formed, avoiding waste of the plant's resources. It is a distinctive feature of flowering plants.

19.9 DEVELOPMENT OF SEED AND FRUIT

After double fertilization the various parts of the flower change:
 - the ZYGOTE grows into the EMBRYO, consisting of an embryonic root (radicle), an embryonic shoot (plumule) and one or two seed leaves (COTYLEDONS);
 - the primary endosperm nucleus develops into the ENDOSPERM, which stores food for the embryo (used up during growth in non-endospermic seeds like pea, or retained in endospermic seeds like maize and castor);
 - the OVULE, with its integuments hardening into the SEED COAT (testa), becomes the SEED; and
 - the OVARY wall ripens into the FRUIT WALL (pericarp), so the whole OVARY becomes the FRUIT enclosing the seeds.
The sepals, petals, stamens and stigma usually wither and fall off. A fruit that develops only from the ovary is a TRUE fruit; when other floral parts such as the thalamus also take part (as in apple) it is a FALSE fruit. Sometimes fruits form without fertilization, giving seedless fruits by PARTHENOCARPY (as in banana).

SIGNIFICANCE OF THE SEED. The seed is a crucial stage in the life of a flowering plant. It contains a dormant embryo protected by a tough seed coat and supplied with stored food, so it can survive unfavourable conditions such as drought and cold and germinate when conditions become suitable. Seeds are the main means of DISPERSAL, carrying the species to new places by wind, water and animals and so reducing competition. Through sexual reproduction the seed also carries new combinations of characters, providing the VARIATION on which natural selection and plant breeding depend. Finally, seeds and the fruits enclosing them are the basis of agriculture and the chief source of food for humans and other animals.

SUMMARY

- Reproduction ensures continuity of a species; it is asexual (one parent, no gametes, identical clones) or sexual (two gametes fuse, offspring show variation).
- Asexual reproduction includes fission (diatoms, bacteria), budding (yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra) and spore formation (Rhizopus, ferns).
- Vegetative propagation grows a new plant from a vegetative part: natural (runners, rhizomes, bulbs, tubers, offsets, leaf buds) and artificial (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture/micropropagation). It gives identical, disease-preserving plants quickly but no variation.
- A flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens = filament + anther) and gynoecium (carpels = stigma + style + ovary with ovules).
- Microsporogenesis: pollen mother cells in the anther undergo meiosis to form tetrads of microspores, which become pollen grains (exine + intine; a vegetative cell and a generative cell that forms two male gametes).
- Megasporogenesis: a megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis to give four megaspores; one survives and forms the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (egg apparatus with egg + 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, and a central cell with two polar nuclei).
- Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma; self (autogamy) or cross (allogamy) by agents - wind (anemophily), water (hydrophily) and insects (entomophily) - each with matching floral adaptations.
- Double fertilization (unique to angiosperms): the pollen tube delivers two male gametes; syngamy (gamete + egg) forms the diploid zygote, and triple fusion (gamete + two polar nuclei) forms the triploid endosperm.
- After fertilization the zygote forms the embryo, the endosperm stores food, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
- The seed protects and nourishes the dormant embryo, allows dispersal to new places, and carries variation; seeds and fruits are the foundation of agriculture.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Reproduction in Plants (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly for short-answer questions and in detail for long-answer questions. Draw and label diagrams where helpful.

questions.question: Distinguish between asexual and sexual reproduction in plants, giving one point of difference and one example of each.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and no fusion of gametes, so the offspring are genetically identical clones of the parent; for example, a new plant growing from the runner of a strawberry. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of a male and a female gamete to form a zygote, so the offspring inherit characters from two parents and show variation; for example, a mango plant grown from a seed formed after fertilization. Thus asexual reproduction gives uniformity and speed, while sexual reproduction gives variation.
questions.explanation: One parent/no gametes/clones vs two gametes/variation, with examples.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe any three methods of natural vegetative propagation, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: (i) Runners (stolons): slender horizontal stems that creep along the ground and strike roots and shoots at their nodes, e.g. grass or strawberry. (ii) Rhizomes: thick underground horizontal stems bearing buds that grow into new shoots, e.g. ginger. (iii) Bulbs: short underground stems with fleshy food-storing leaf bases and buds that form new plants, e.g. onion. (Tubers such as the potato, with buds in its 'eyes', and offsets as in water hyacinth are other examples.)
questions.explanation: Runner, rhizome, bulb (or tuber/offset) with descriptions and examples.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a typical flower, naming its four whorls from outside inwards and the function of each.
questions.answer: A typical flower is borne on a stalk (pedicel) that widens into the thalamus, on which four whorls are arranged from outside inwards. (1) Calyx: the outermost whorl of green, leaf-like sepals that protect the young flower in the bud and may photosynthesise. (2) Corolla: the whorl of petals, usually brightly coloured and scented, which attracts insects and other pollinators. (3) Androecium: the male whorl of stamens, each with a filament bearing a two-lobed anther in which pollen grains are produced. (4) Gynoecium: the female whorl of carpels, each having a swollen ovary containing ovules, a slender style, and a sticky stigma that receives pollen. The calyx and corolla are accessory whorls, while the androecium and gynoecium are the essential whorls that produce the gametes.
questions.explanation: Four whorls (calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium) with parts and functions.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a mature pollen grain.
questions.answer: A mature pollen grain has a two-layered wall: a tough, sculptured outer layer called the exine, made of resistant sporopollenin and pierced by thin germ pores, and a thin inner layer called the intine, made of cellulose and pectin. Inside, the pollen grain (the male gametophyte) contains two cells: a large vegetative (tube) cell and a small generative cell. The generative cell later divides to form two male gametes. The pollen tube emerges through a germ pore during germination.
questions.explanation: Exine, intine, germ pore, vegetative and generative cells, two male gametes.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the mature embryo sac of a flowering plant.
questions.answer: The mature embryo sac (female gametophyte) is a seven-celled, eight-nucleate structure inside the ovule. At the micropylar end lies the egg apparatus of three cells - one egg cell (the female gamete) flanked by two synergids. At the opposite chalazal end are three antipodal cells. In the centre is a large central cell containing two polar nuclei, which fuse to form the diploid secondary nucleus. Thus there are seven cells but eight nuclei. The egg is fertilized by one male gamete and the polar nuclei by the other.
questions.explanation: 7 cells, 8 nuclei: egg apparatus, antipodals, central cell with polar nuclei.

questions.question: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination, and give one advantage of each.
questions.answer: Self-pollination (autogamy) is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant; it occurs in bisexual flowers, keeps the parental characters pure and ensures seed set even when pollinators are scarce. Cross-pollination (allogamy) is the transfer of pollen to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species; it introduces variation and produces more vigorous, better-adapted offspring. So self-pollination gives certainty and purity, while cross-pollination gives variation and vigour.
questions.explanation: Same plant vs different plant; purity/certainty vs variation/vigour.

questions.question: List four features of a wind-pollinated (anemophilous) flower.
questions.answer: Wind-pollinated flowers are (i) small, dull-coloured and inconspicuous; (ii) without scent and without nectar; (iii) producers of large amounts of light, dry, smooth pollen that is easily carried by wind; and (iv) provided with well-exposed stamens (versatile anthers) and large, often feathery stigmas that catch the drifting pollen. Grasses, maize and many trees are wind-pollinated.
questions.explanation: Small dull scentless flowers; abundant light pollen; feathery stigmas; exposed anthers.

questions.question: Explain the process of double fertilization in angiosperms and state its significance.
questions.answer: After pollination, the pollen grain on the stigma germinates and puts out a pollen tube that grows down through the style and enters the embryo sac, usually through the micropyle. The tube carries the two male gametes and discharges them into the embryo sac, where two fusions occur - hence double fertilization. In syngamy (true fertilization) one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form the diploid zygote (2n), which develops into the embryo. In triple fusion the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form the triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm that nourishes the embryo. Because both fusions occur together, endosperm (food) is produced only when an embryo is also formed, so no resources are wasted. Double fertilization is a feature unique to flowering plants (angiosperms).
questions.explanation: Pollen tube, two gametes; syngamy -> zygote; triple fusion -> endosperm; unique, avoids waste.

questions.question: After fertilization, what do the following develop into: (a) zygote, (b) primary endosperm nucleus, (c) ovule, (d) ovary?
questions.answer: (a) The zygote develops into the embryo (with radicle, plumule and cotyledons). (b) The primary endosperm nucleus develops into the endosperm, the food-storing tissue. (c) The ovule, with its integuments hardening into the seed coat, becomes the seed. (d) The ovary wall ripens into the pericarp, so the whole ovary becomes the fruit enclosing the seeds. The sepals, petals and stamens usually wither and fall.
questions.explanation: Zygote->embryo; PEN->endosperm; ovule->seed; ovary->fruit.

questions.question: Why is double fertilization considered advantageous, and what is the significance of the seed formed after it? Discuss.
questions.answer: Double fertilization is advantageous because the two fusions are coordinated: syngamy forms the zygote (future embryo) and triple fusion forms the endosperm (its food) at the same time. Thus the plant invests in food-storing endosperm only when an embryo is actually produced, avoiding the waste of resources on unfertilized ovules; the triploid endosperm also provides rich nourishment for the growing embryo. The seed that results is highly significant: its tough seed coat and stored food let the dormant embryo survive unfavourable conditions such as drought and cold, germinating only when conditions are suitable. Seeds are the chief means of dispersal, carrying the species to new areas by wind, water and animals and reducing competition. Because they are formed by sexual reproduction, seeds also carry new combinations of characters, supplying the variation on which natural selection and plant breeding depend. Finally, seeds and fruits form the foundation of agriculture and the main source of food.
questions.explanation: Coordinated fusions save resources; endosperm nourishes; seed protects, disperses, varies, feeds.

questions.question: Define asexual reproduction and give one example.
questions.answer: Asexual reproduction is the production of new individuals from a single parent without the formation or fusion of gametes; the offspring are genetically identical to the parent. For example, yeast reproduces asexually by budding, and Spirogyra by fragmentation.
questions.explanation: One parent, no gametes, identical offspring; example.

questions.question: Explain fragmentation and spore formation as methods of asexual reproduction, with one example each.
questions.answer: In fragmentation the body of the organism breaks into two or more fragments, and each fragment grows into a complete new organism; for example, the filamentous alga Spirogyra breaks into pieces that each form a new filament. In spore formation the organism produces many tiny, thick-walled spores inside a sporangium; each spore is dispersed and germinates into a new plant without fusing with any other cell, as in the bread mould Rhizopus and in ferns.
questions.explanation: Fragmentation (Spirogyra) and spore formation (Rhizopus/ferns).

questions.question: What is vegetative propagation? Name the plant part involved in propagation by (a) rhizome and (b) bulb.
questions.answer: Vegetative propagation is a form of asexual reproduction in which a vegetative part of the plant - a root, stem, leaf or bud - grows into a new, independent plant identical to the parent. (a) A rhizome is an underground horizontal stem (as in ginger). (b) A bulb is a short underground stem with fleshy leaf bases (as in onion).
questions.explanation: Definition; rhizome = underground stem; bulb = short underground stem.

questions.question: State three advantages of vegetative propagation.
questions.answer: (i) It is quicker than growing plants from seed. (ii) The new plants are genetically identical to the parent, so desirable qualities (taste, colour, disease resistance) are retained. (iii) It allows plants that produce few or no viable seeds - such as banana, sugarcane and seedless grapes - to be multiplied. (An added advantage is that many identical plants can be produced from a single parent.)
questions.explanation: Speed, identical quality retention, propagation of seedless plants.

questions.question: Name the four whorls of a typical flower in order from outside inwards.
questions.answer: From outside inwards the four whorls of a flower are: (1) calyx (sepals), (2) corolla (petals), (3) androecium (stamens) and (4) gynoecium (carpels). The calyx and corolla are accessory whorls; the androecium and gynoecium are the essential reproductive whorls.
questions.explanation: Calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium.

questions.question: Distinguish between the accessory and the essential whorls of a flower.
questions.answer: The accessory whorls are the calyx (sepals) and the corolla (petals); they do not produce gametes but assist reproduction - the calyx protects the bud and the corolla attracts pollinators. The essential whorls are the androecium (stamens) and the gynoecium (carpels); they are essential because they actually produce the male and female gametes needed for sexual reproduction.
questions.explanation: Accessory (calyx, corolla) aid; essential (androecium, gynoecium) make gametes.

questions.question: Name the parts of (a) a stamen and (b) a carpel.
questions.answer: (a) A stamen has two parts: a stalk called the filament and a two-lobed anther at its tip in which pollen grains are produced. (b) A carpel has three parts: a sticky stigma that receives pollen, a slender style, and a swollen basal ovary that contains the ovules.
questions.explanation: Stamen = filament + anther; carpel = stigma + style + ovary.

questions.question: State the functions of the calyx and the corolla.
questions.answer: The calyx, made of green sepals, protects the young flower while it is still a bud and, being green, may also carry out some photosynthesis. The corolla, made of brightly coloured and often scented petals rich in nectar, attracts insects and other pollinators to the flower and so helps in pollination.
questions.explanation: Calyx protects bud; corolla attracts pollinators.

questions.question: What is microsporogenesis?
questions.answer: Microsporogenesis is the process of formation of microspores (pollen grains) inside the anther. The diploid pollen mother cells in the pollen sacs of the anther undergo meiosis, each forming a tetrad of four haploid microspores, which separate and develop into pollen grains.
questions.explanation: Formation of pollen by meiosis of pollen mother cells.

questions.question: Describe the wall layers of a pollen grain and their features.
questions.answer: A pollen grain has a two-layered wall. The outer layer, the exine, is thick, tough and often sculptured; it is made of a very resistant substance called sporopollenin and has thin areas called germ pores through which the pollen tube later emerges. The inner layer, the intine, is thin and made of cellulose and pectin, lying next to the cytoplasm. The tough exine protects the delicate contents during dispersal.
questions.explanation: Exine (sporopollenin, germ pores) and intine (cellulose/pectin).

questions.question: Name the two cells present in a mature pollen grain and state the fate of each.
questions.answer: A mature pollen grain contains a large vegetative (tube) cell and a small generative cell. The vegetative cell forms the pollen tube that grows down the style, while the generative cell divides to form the two male gametes that are carried by the tube to the embryo sac.
questions.explanation: Vegetative cell -> pollen tube; generative cell -> two male gametes.

questions.question: Label the main parts of an ovule.
questions.answer: An ovule is attached to the ovary by a stalk called the funicle. Its main body is the nucellus, surrounded by one or two protective integuments that leave a small opening, the micropyle, at one end. The point where the funicle, integuments and nucellus meet is the chalaza. The embryo sac lies within the nucellus.
questions.explanation: Funicle, nucellus, integuments, micropyle, chalaza.

questions.question: Describe how the embryo sac is formed from the megaspore mother cell.
questions.answer: Within the nucellus of the ovule a single diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores arranged in a row. Usually three of them degenerate and only one functional megaspore survives. This megaspore enlarges and its nucleus divides mitotically three times to give eight nuclei, which organise into the seven-celled, eight-nucleate mature embryo sac - the egg apparatus, the antipodal cells and the central cell with two polar nuclei.
questions.explanation: Meiosis -> 4 megaspores; 1 survives; 3 mitoses -> 8 nuclei -> embryo sac.

questions.question: Name the cells present at the micropylar and chalazal ends of the embryo sac.
questions.answer: At the micropylar end of the embryo sac lies the egg apparatus, made of one egg cell flanked by two synergids. At the opposite chalazal end are the three antipodal cells. In the centre lies the large central cell with two polar nuclei.
questions.explanation: Micropylar: egg + 2 synergids; chalazal: 3 antipodals; centre: 2 polar nuclei.

questions.question: Define pollination and name its two types.
questions.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma. Its two types are self-pollination (autogamy), the transfer of pollen to the stigma of the same flower or another flower of the same plant, and cross-pollination (allogamy), the transfer of pollen to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.
questions.explanation: Definition; self (autogamy) and cross (allogamy).

questions.question: List the features of insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers.
questions.answer: Insect-pollinated flowers are usually large or borne in clusters and are brightly coloured to be conspicuous. They are scented and produce nectar as a reward for the visiting insect. Their pollen grains are sticky or spiny and their stigmas are sticky, so pollen clings to the insect's body and is carried from flower to flower. Common insect pollinators are bees, butterflies, moths and beetles.
questions.explanation: Large, coloured, scented, nectar, sticky pollen and stigma.

questions.question: Give two devices by which flowers favour cross-pollination.
questions.answer: Flowers favour cross-pollination by (i) bearing unisexual flowers, so pollen from one flower must reach another; and (ii) having the anthers and the stigma mature at different times, so that self-pollen cannot reach the same flower's stigma. Self-incompatibility, where a plant's own pollen cannot fertilize its ovules, is another such device.
questions.explanation: Unisexual flowers; different maturation times; self-incompatibility.

questions.question: What is a pollen tube and what does it carry?
questions.answer: A pollen tube is the tubular outgrowth produced when a pollen grain germinates on the stigma. It grows down through the style towards the ovule and enters the embryo sac, usually through the micropyle. The pollen tube carries the two male gametes to the embryo sac for fertilization.
questions.explanation: Outgrowth of germinating pollen; carries two male gametes.

questions.question: Explain syngamy and triple fusion.
questions.answer: Both are fusions that occur inside the embryo sac during double fertilization. In syngamy (true fertilization) one male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid (2n) zygote, which develops into the embryo. In triple fusion the second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to form a triploid (3n) primary endosperm nucleus, which develops into the endosperm that nourishes the embryo.
questions.explanation: Syngamy: gamete + egg -> 2n zygote; triple fusion: gamete + 2 polar nuclei -> 3n endosperm.

questions.question: State what the seed coat and the endosperm develop from and their roles.
questions.answer: The seed coat (testa) develops from the integuments of the ovule and forms a tough protective covering around the seed. The endosperm develops from the primary endosperm nucleus (formed by triple fusion) and is a nutritive tissue that stores food to nourish the developing embryo during germination.
questions.explanation: Seed coat from integuments (protection); endosperm from PEN (nourishment).

questions.question: Why is double fertilization considered advantageous to angiosperms?
questions.answer: Double fertilization is advantageous because its two fusions are coordinated: syngamy forms the zygote (the future embryo) and triple fusion forms the endosperm (the embryo's food) at the same time. As a result the plant develops food-storing endosperm only when an embryo is actually formed, so it does not waste resources on unfertilized ovules. The triploid endosperm also provides a rich, ready supply of nourishment for the growing embryo, improving the chances that the seed will germinate successfully.
questions.explanation: Coordinated fusions: endosperm only with embryo, saving resources; rich nutrition.

questions.question: Trace the changes that occur in a flower after fertilization to form a fruit with seeds.
questions.answer: After double fertilization several floral parts change. The zygote grows into the embryo (radicle, plumule and cotyledons); the primary endosperm nucleus develops into the food-storing endosperm; the integuments of the ovule harden into the seed coat, so the whole ovule becomes the seed; and the ovary wall ripens into the pericarp, so the ovary becomes the fruit enclosing the seeds. Meanwhile the sepals, petals, stamens and stigma usually wither and fall off.
questions.explanation: Zygote->embryo, PEN->endosperm, ovule->seed, ovary->fruit; other parts fall.

questions.question: Describe the various methods of artificial vegetative propagation with one example of each.
questions.answer: Artificial vegetative propagation is practised by gardeners to multiply useful plants quickly while keeping their qualities unchanged. (1) Cutting: a piece of stem, root or leaf bearing buds is cut and planted; it develops roots and grows into a new plant, as in rose and sugarcane. (2) Layering: a lower branch is bent to the ground and part of it is covered with moist soil; after it forms roots, the rooted portion is cut from the parent and grown separately, as in jasmine and guava. (3) Grafting: parts of two plants are joined so they unite and grow as one; the rooted lower plant is the stock and the inserted shoot is the scion, combining a strong root system with a desirable fruit, as in mango and apple. (4) Tissue culture (micropropagation): small pieces of tissue (explants) are grown on a sterile nutrient medium with hormones; because plant cells are totipotent, thousands of identical plantlets are raised from a little tissue, as in orchids and banana.
questions.explanation: Cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture with examples.

questions.question: With the help of the four whorls, describe the structure of a typical bisexual flower and classify the whorls as accessory or essential.
questions.answer: A typical bisexual flower is borne on a stalk (pedicel) that widens into the thalamus, on which four whorls are arranged from outside inwards. The calyx is the outermost whorl of green sepals that protect the bud. The corolla is the whorl of brightly coloured, often scented petals that attract pollinators. The androecium is the male whorl of stamens; each stamen has a filament and a two-lobed anther that produces pollen grains. The gynoecium is the female whorl of carpels; each carpel has a sticky stigma, a slender style, and a swollen ovary containing ovules. Of these, the calyx and corolla are accessory whorls because they only assist reproduction, while the androecium and gynoecium are essential whorls because they produce the male and female gametes. A flower bearing both androecium and gynoecium is bisexual, and one with all four whorls is complete.
questions.explanation: Four whorls with parts and functions; accessory vs essential; bisexual/complete.

questions.question: Explain the process of microsporogenesis and describe the structure of a pollen grain.
questions.answer: Microsporogenesis is the formation of microspores (pollen grains) in the anther. A young anther is four-lobed and contains four pollen sacs (microsporangia), each packed with diploid pollen mother cells. Each pollen mother cell undergoes meiosis, forming a tetrad of four haploid microspores. The microspores separate, enlarge and develop into pollen grains. A mature pollen grain has a two-layered wall: a tough, sculptured outer exine of resistant sporopollenin bearing germ pores, and a thin inner intine of cellulose and pectin. Inside, the pollen grain (the male gametophyte) contains a large vegetative (tube) cell and a small generative cell; the generative cell later divides to form the two male gametes. Pollen grains are light and produced in large numbers, aiding dispersal.
questions.explanation: Meiosis of pollen mother cells -> tetrads -> pollen; exine, intine, two cells.

questions.question: Describe megasporogenesis and the structure of the mature embryo sac.
questions.answer: Megasporogenesis is the formation of the megaspore, and hence the embryo sac, inside the ovule. The ovule is attached by a funicle and consists of a nucellus surrounded by integuments that leave a micropyle. Within the nucellus a single diploid megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores in a row. Usually three degenerate and only one functional megaspore survives. The nucleus of this megaspore divides mitotically three times to give eight nuclei, which organise into the mature embryo sac. The embryo sac is seven-celled and eight-nucleate: at the micropylar end lies the egg apparatus (one egg cell and two synergids); at the chalazal end lie three antipodal cells; and in the centre is a large central cell containing two polar nuclei that fuse to form the diploid secondary nucleus. The egg is later fertilized by one male gamete and the polar nuclei by the other.
questions.explanation: Ovule; meiosis -> 4 megaspores; 1 survives; 3 mitoses -> 8 nuclei; 7-celled sac parts.

questions.question: Compare the adaptations of wind-pollinated and insect-pollinated flowers.
questions.answer: Wind-pollinated (anemophilous) and insect-pollinated (entomophilous) flowers show clearly contrasting adaptations. Wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull-coloured and inconspicuous, without scent or nectar, because they need not attract any animal. They produce enormous quantities of light, dry, smooth pollen that is easily carried by the wind, and have well-exposed stamens (versatile anthers) and large, often feathery stigmas that catch drifting pollen; grasses and maize are examples. Insect-pollinated flowers, in contrast, are large or clustered, brightly coloured, scented, and produce nectar as a reward to attract insects. Their pollen grains are fewer but sticky or spiny, and their stigmas are sticky, so pollen clings to the insect's body and is carried from flower to flower. Thus each type of flower is adapted to its particular pollinating agent to improve the chance of successful pollination.
questions.explanation: Contrast size, colour, scent, nectar, pollen and stigma for wind vs insects.

questions.question: Explain the events from pollination to the formation of the seed and fruit in a flowering plant.
questions.answer: After pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, the pollen grain germinates and puts out a pollen tube that grows down through the style and enters the embryo sac, usually through the micropyle, carrying two male gametes. There double fertilization occurs: in syngamy one gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, and in triple fusion the other gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. The zygote then develops into the embryo (radicle, plumule and cotyledons), while the primary endosperm nucleus develops into the food-storing endosperm. The integuments of the ovule harden into the seed coat, so the whole ovule becomes the seed, and the ovary wall ripens into the pericarp, so the ovary becomes the fruit enclosing the seeds. The sepals, petals and stamens usually wither and fall away.
questions.explanation: Pollen tube, double fertilization, embryo/endosperm, ovule->seed, ovary->fruit.

questions.question: 'Double fertilization is a unique and useful event in angiosperms.' Discuss this statement and explain the significance of the seed.
questions.answer: Double fertilization is unique to flowering plants (angiosperms) because two fusions take place in the embryo sac from the two male gametes brought by one pollen tube: syngamy, in which a gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote, and triple fusion, in which the other gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm. It is useful because these events are coordinated, so nutritive endosperm is formed only when an embryo is also formed - the plant does not waste resources, and the embryo is supplied with rich food. The seed that results is highly significant. Its tough seed coat and stored food allow the dormant embryo to survive unfavourable conditions such as drought and cold and to germinate when conditions become suitable. Seeds are the main means of dispersal, spreading the species to new places by wind, water and animals and so reducing competition. Being products of sexual reproduction, seeds carry new combinations of characters, supplying the variation needed for adaptation and plant breeding. Finally, seeds and the fruits enclosing them are the foundation of agriculture and the chief source of food.
questions.explanation: Uniqueness and economy of double fertilization; seed protection, dispersal, variation, food.

questions.question: Describe fission, budding, fragmentation and spore formation as methods of asexual reproduction, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: Fission is the division of a unicellular parent into daughter cells: in binary fission two daughters are formed and in multiple fission many, as in diatoms and bacteria. Budding is the formation of a small outgrowth, or bud, on the parent body that grows and separates as a new individual, as in yeast. Fragmentation is the breaking of the body into two or more fragments, each of which grows into a complete organism, as in the alga Spirogyra. Spore formation is the production of many tiny, thick-walled spores in a sporangium; each spore is dispersed and germinates into a new plant without fusing with any other cell, as in the mould Rhizopus and in ferns. All four are asexual, needing one parent and producing identical offspring.
questions.explanation: Fission (diatoms), budding (yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), spores (Rhizopus).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A gardener wants to multiply a prize rose and a mango tree of excellent fruit quality. He takes stem cuttings of the rose, and for the mango he joins a shoot of the good tree onto the rooted stem of an ordinary seedling. He notices that all the new plants have exactly the qualities of the parents.
(a) Name the method used for the rose.
(b) Name the method used for the mango and identify the stock and the scion.
(c) Why do the new plants have exactly the parents' qualities?
(d) State one advantage of these methods over growing plants from seed.
questions.answer: (a) The rose is multiplied by cutting - a piece of stem with buds is planted and grows roots. (b) The mango is multiplied by grafting; the rooted ordinary seedling is the stock and the shoot of the good tree inserted onto it is the scion. (c) Because these are methods of vegetative (asexual) propagation, no gametes are involved and the new plants are genetically identical clones of the parent, so they keep exactly the parents' qualities. (d) They are quicker than growing from seed and, unlike seedlings, reliably retain the desirable qualities (and let plants with poor or no seeds be multiplied).
questions.explanation: Cutting; grafting (stock/scion); clones keep quality; speed and reliability.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a pond, the filamentous alga Spirogyra breaks into pieces after a storm, and soon many new filaments appear. Nearby, yeast in a sugary solution forms small outgrowths that later separate. In moist bread, a mould produces black sporangia full of tiny spores.
(a) Name the method of reproduction in Spirogyra.
(b) Name the method of reproduction in yeast.
(c) What are the tiny structures in the mould's sporangia and how do they help?
(d) Are the offspring in these cases identical or variable? Why?
questions.answer: (a) Spirogyra reproduces by fragmentation - each broken piece grows into a new filament. (b) Yeast reproduces by budding - a bud forms, grows and separates. (c) They are spores; being light and thick-walled they are dispersed by wind or water and germinate into new moulds, also helping the organism survive bad conditions. (d) The offspring are genetically identical, because all these are asexual methods with a single parent and no fusion of gametes.
questions.explanation: Fragmentation; budding; spores disperse/survive; identical (asexual).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student examines a hibiscus flower. She finds an outer whorl of green leaf-like parts, then a whorl of large red petals, then a set of stalked structures with knob-like tips carrying yellow powder, and finally a central structure with a sticky top, a stalk and a swollen base.
(a) Name the four whorls she observes in order.
(b) What is the yellow powder and where is it produced?
(c) Name the three parts of the central female structure.
(d) Which two whorls are the essential whorls and why?
questions.answer: (a) In order she observes the calyx (green sepals), the corolla (red petals), the androecium (stamens) and the gynoecium (carpel). (b) The yellow powder is pollen grains, produced in the anthers of the stamens. (c) The central female structure (carpel) has three parts: the sticky stigma at the top, the slender style, and the swollen ovary at the base. (d) The androecium and the gynoecium are the essential whorls, because they produce the male and female gametes needed for sexual reproduction, while the calyx and corolla only assist.
questions.explanation: Four whorls; pollen in anthers; stigma/style/ovary; essential = androecium+gynoecium.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Inside a young anther are four pollen sacs packed with diploid cells. As the anther matures, each of these cells divides in a special way to give groups of four cells, which then develop thick walls and become the yellow dust released when the anther splits.
(a) What are the diploid cells called?
(b) By what type of division do they form groups of four?
(c) What is a group of four such cells called?
(d) Name the two wall layers of the mature grain.
questions.answer: (a) The diploid cells are the pollen mother cells (microspore mother cells). (b) They divide by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number. (c) A group of four resulting microspores is called a tetrad. (d) The mature pollen grain has two wall layers: a tough outer exine (of sporopollenin, with germ pores) and a thin inner intine (of cellulose and pectin).
questions.explanation: Pollen mother cells; meiosis; tetrad; exine and intine.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Inside an ovule, one large diploid cell divides to give four cells in a row. Three of these break down and one survives; its nucleus then divides repeatedly until a structure with seven cells and eight nuclei is formed. This structure contains the female gamete.
(a) Name the large diploid cell.
(b) What type of division first gives the four cells?
(c) How many nuclei are present in the mature structure, and what is it called?
(d) Name the female gamete and the two cells beside it.
questions.answer: (a) The large diploid cell is the megaspore mother cell. (b) It divides by meiosis to give four haploid megaspores. (c) The mature structure has eight nuclei (in seven cells) and is called the embryo sac (female gametophyte). (d) The female gamete is the egg cell, and it is flanked by two synergids, together forming the egg apparatus.
questions.explanation: Megaspore mother cell; meiosis; embryo sac (8 nuclei); egg + 2 synergids.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two plants grow side by side. Plant A has small, dull, scentless flowers producing masses of light dry pollen and large feathery stigmas. Plant B has large, bright, scented flowers with nectar and sticky pollen.
(a) Name the likely pollinating agent of plant A.
(b) Name the likely pollinating agent of plant B.
(c) For each plant, give one feature that suits its pollinator.
(d) Which plant is more likely to be cross-pollinated by animals, and why?
questions.answer: (a) Plant A is likely pollinated by wind (anemophily). (b) Plant B is likely pollinated by insects (entomophily). (c) Plant A's masses of light dry pollen and large feathery stigmas suit wind pollination; plant B's bright scented flowers with nectar and sticky pollen suit insect pollination. (d) Plant B is more likely to be cross-pollinated by animals, because its colour, scent, nectar and sticky pollen attract insects that carry pollen from flower to flower.
questions.explanation: Wind vs insects; matching features; B attracts animal pollinators.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a pea plant the flower pollinates itself before it even opens, using its own pollen. In an aquatic plant like Vallisneria, pollen is carried by water to the stigma of a flower on another plant.
(a) Name the type of pollination in the pea.
(b) Name the type of pollination in Vallisneria and the agent involved.
(c) Give one advantage of the pea's type of pollination.
(d) Give one advantage of the Vallisneria's type of pollination.
questions.answer: (a) In the pea it is self-pollination (autogamy), as its own pollen reaches its own stigma. (b) In Vallisneria it is cross-pollination, and the agent is water (hydrophily). (c) Self-pollination keeps the parental characters pure and ensures seed set even when pollinators are absent. (d) Cross-pollination introduces variation and produces more vigorous, better-adapted offspring.
questions.explanation: Self (autogamy); cross by water; purity/certainty vs variation/vigour.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A pollen grain lands on a stigma, germinates, and sends a tube down the style into the embryo sac, carrying two male gametes. One gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the two polar nuclei. Later the flower forms a fruit with seeds.
(a) What is the tube called and what does it carry?
(b) Name the fusion of a male gamete with the egg and the product formed.
(c) Name the fusion with the two polar nuclei and the product formed.
(d) State what the ovule and the ovary develop into.
questions.answer: (a) The tube is the pollen tube; it carries the two male gametes to the embryo sac. (b) The fusion of a male gamete with the egg is syngamy, forming the diploid zygote (which becomes the embryo). (c) The fusion of the second gamete with the two polar nuclei is triple fusion, forming the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (which becomes the endosperm). (d) The ovule develops into the seed and the ovary develops into the fruit.
questions.explanation: Pollen tube/two gametes; syngamy->zygote; triple fusion->endosperm; ovule->seed, ovary->fruit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In flowering plants two male gametes are used: one forms the zygote and the other forms a nutritive tissue. This coordinated event does not occur in non-flowering plants. The seed that forms carries a dormant embryo, stored food and a tough coat.
(a) Name this coordinated event and the group of plants in which it occurs.
(b) Why is it economical for the plant?
(c) State the ploidy of the zygote and of the nutritive tissue.
(d) Give two ways in which the seed helps the plant.
questions.answer: (a) The event is double fertilization, and it occurs only in angiosperms (flowering plants). (b) It is economical because the nutritive endosperm is formed only when an embryo is also formed, so the plant does not waste resources on unfertilized ovules. (c) The zygote is diploid (2n) and the nutritive tissue (endosperm) is triploid (3n). (d) The seed protects and nourishes the dormant embryo so it survives unfavourable conditions, and it helps disperse the species to new places (also carrying variation from sexual reproduction).
questions.explanation: Double fertilization in angiosperms; economical; 2n zygote, 3n endosperm; seed protects/disperses.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A maize seed cut open shows a large starchy region and a small embryo, while a pea seed has two thick seed leaves and only a trace of the starchy region. A banana fruit, however, has no seeds at all.
(a) Name the starchy food-storing tissue in the maize seed.
(b) In the pea, where is the food mainly stored?
(c) Which of these two is an endospermic seed?
(d) Suggest why the banana has no seeds.
questions.answer: (a) The starchy food-storing tissue in maize is the endosperm. (b) In the pea the food is mainly stored in the two thick seed leaves, the cotyledons, as the endosperm is used up during development. (c) The maize seed is the endospermic (albuminous) seed, since it retains its endosperm at maturity. (d) The banana has no seeds because its fruit develops without fertilization, by parthenocarpy, so no seeds are formed.
questions.explanation: Endosperm; cotyledons; maize endospermic; banana parthenocarpic.
